entries.title: How tiny animals build coral reefs
entries.answer: A coral reef can look like a pile of rocks or plants, but it is built by small animals called coral polyps. Many kinds live in groups. The kinds that build reefs make hard cups around themselves. Old cups stay behind and new ones can grow on top, so a reef gets larger over time. Many reef corals also have tiny algae living inside them. The algae use sunlight to make food, and the coral gets some of that food. The reef’s holes and branches give fish and other animals places to live.
facts: A coral reef can shelter many different living things.
Heat stress can cause coral to lose its partner algae and turn pale.

entries.title: What makes ocean currents flow
entries.answer: An ocean current is water moving from one place to another. In shallow areas near the coast, the tide can make water flow into a bay and later flow out. Farther from land, winds can drive large streams of water near the surface. Cold or salty water is usually denser than warmer or fresher water. That difference also helps move water around, including deep below the ocean’s surface. These currents can carry heat between regions, so they help shape weather and climate on land.
facts: Winds, tides, and differences in water density all drive ocean currents.
The Gulf Stream carries warm water in the Atlantic Ocean.

entries.title: Why the ocean has tides
entries.answer: If you leave a stick on the beach, later waves might reach it even though the wind has not changed. The water level rises and falls as part of the tide. The Moon’s pull on Earth and the ocean is a major cause, and the Sun’s pull matters too. The water does not go up and down by the same amount on every shore. The shape of the coast and depth of the water make a difference. Many places have two high tides and two low tides in about a day.
facts: High tide and low tide are different water levels.
A tide can also make water flow sideways through a narrow channel.

entries.title: Why there are waves in the ocean
entries.answer: Many ocean waves begin when wind pushes on the water’s surface. The pushes add energy. That energy can travel a long way as a wave, even when much of the water just moves around its own small area. Near a beach, waves slow down as the water gets shallower. Their tops can tip forward and break, making the white water you see at the shore. A different kind of wave, called a tsunami, can start when the ocean is suddenly disturbed, such as when an earthquake moves the sea floor.
facts: Wind waves can travel far from the place where the wind made them.
Where waves break, they can stir up and move sand.
